title: Why Reminders Make Classroom Management More Difficult ent-more-difficult/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin identifies reactive reminders — restating expectations after misbehavior has already occurred — as the most common classroom management mistake teachers make. He explains that every reminder given instead of enforcing a consequence undermines a classroom management plan, teaching students that directions are merely suggestions until a teacher's tone or mood escalates. This erodes the power of a teacher's words, since students learn to gauge urgency by frequency of repetition rather than by what's actually said. The fix is to eliminate reminders entirely, following the classroom management plan as written, even though the transition will be difficult and shocking at first. He promises this single change leads to dramatic behavior improvement as students learn a teacher's words carry real weight, and previews a companion article on how to give a reminder that actually helps.
points: Giving a reminder after misbehavior instead of enforcing a consequence undermines a teacher's classroom management plan.
Frequent reminders teach students that directions are optional suggestions rather than firm expectations.
Students learn to gauge real urgency by a teacher's tone or repetition rather than by the words themselves, weakening the teacher's voice.
Eliminating post-misbehavior reminders entirely, in favor of following the management plan as written, leads to dramatic improvement over time.
The transition away from reminders will be difficult at first, with rough early days before students adjust.
quotes: If there is one classroom management mistake made more often than others, it is the practice of giving reminders after misbehavior has already occurred.
Every time you give a reminder in response to misbehavior, you fail to follow through with your classroom management plan.
So naturally when you ask them to line up quietly with their hands at their sides, to them it doesn’t really mean you expect them to do it—at least not the first time you ask.

When your first reaction to misbehavior is to give a reminder, you’re communicating to your students that you don’t really mean what you say—unless, that is, you raise your voice, lose your cool, or otherwise show your frustration.
If you give a lot of reminders, your words won’t pack any punch. Your voice will no more cut through the static in their heads than the soft drone of a Hummingbird outside your classroom window.

If you just make this one change, if you decide that you’re no longer going to give post-misbehavior reminders—and instead follow your classroom management plan as it’s written—you will notice dramatic improvement in behavior.
